intro: The Shiv Tandav Stotram is a Sanskrit hymn in praise of Shiva, composed as a series of sixteen verses of unusually dense, rolling rhythm meant to mirror the tandava, Shiva's dance of creation and dissolution. Tradition attributes its authorship to Ravana, the Lanka king of the Ramayana, said to have composed it as an act of devotion and surrender to Shiva. No historical date is recorded for the text; it has simply been passed down as part of Shiva devotional literature. The hymn moves between vivid physical description of Shiva - his matted hair, the Ganga flowing through it, the crescent moon, the snake ornaments - and philosophical reflection on detachment, equanimity, and liberation. It closes with a verse stating what reciting it is said to bring. This page explains what each portion of the verses is about, without reproducing them line by line, and how the text is used in practice today.

groups.heading: Shiva's dance and his matted hair
groups.body: The opening verses describe Shiva in motion, performing his wild tandava dance, with the Ganga cascading through his piled, matted locks and his garland of serpents swinging with the movement. The imagery is almost cinematic - sound syllables like 'dhimi dhimi' are used to recreate the beat of a damaru drum. These lines are not narrating a story so much as building a mental picture of Shiva as cosmic dancer, forceful and unceasing, with the river and the moon caught in his hair as fixed details repeated across the stotra.

groups.heading: The crescent moon and Parvati
groups.body: Several verses turn to Shiva's calmer aspect - the young moon resting on his head, his face lit by both moonlight and the fire at his third eye. Alongside this, the text brings in Parvati, called here the daughter of the mountain, describing the couple's closeness in poetic, affectionate language. These verses hold together Shiva's fierce and gentle sides without resolving them into one simple picture, which is part of what the Shiv Tandav Stotram is doing throughout - stacking contrasting images of the same god.

groups.heading: Ash, skulls, and the destroyer of fear
groups.body: A cluster of verses describes Shiva's appearance as an ascetic - ash-smeared, garlanded with skulls, dwelling among cremation grounds, indifferent to comfort or ornament. Rather than being grim, this is presented as a mark of Shiva's freedom from convention and fear. The text lists him as the destroyer of various named demons and obstacles, including the destroyer of desire, of the three cities, and of worldly bondage, using each as another name under which he is addressed.

groups.heading: The refrain: ender of endings
groups.body: A pair of matching verses repeats the same list of Shiva's conquests twice, first calling him the 'cutter' and then the 'ender' of each threat - desire, the three cities, worldly existence, sacrifice-pride, the elephant demon, and death itself. This doubled refrain is one of the most recognisable passages of the Shiv Tandav Stotram, often sung on its own because of how it builds rhythmically through repetition before returning to the description of Shiva's dance.

groups.heading: Equanimity and longing for simplicity
groups.body: Here the voice of the hymn shifts to something more personal. The speaker asks when he will attain evenness of mind - seeing a stone bed and a jewelled one as the same, a friend and an enemy as the same, a blade of grass and a king as the same. He wishes to live simply near the Ganga, free of restless thought, chanting Shiva's name. This section reads less like description of Shiva and more like a prayer for inner steadiness, attributed in tradition to Ravana's own longing despite his power and position.

groups.heading: Shiva's festive, auspicious form
groups.body: The later verses return to celebratory description - the fragrance of jasmine flowers offered by celestial women, the sound of conch-shells and chanting at Shiva's wedding, and language about Shiva's name bringing good fortune and victory to the world. These verses are more ornamental in style, piling up images of abundance and festivity around Shiva rather than making a single argument.

groups.heading: The closing declaration
groups.body: The final two verses step outside the praise itself and speak about the hymn as an object. The text states that one who recites, remembers, or even just utters it becomes purified, and that devotion to the guru and to Shiva follows from this practice, as opposed to other paths. The very last verse specifically credits Ravana with composing it and praying it at the close of his evening worship of Shiva, which is why many readers treat the Shiv Tandav Stotram as something recited at the end of a Shiva puja rather than at the start.

recitation: The Shiv Tandav Stotram is commonly recited during Shiva worship, particularly in the evening, since the closing verse of the text itself refers to reciting it at the end of worship during twilight hours, called pradosha. It is heard widely on Maha Shivaratri, when many temples and households keep an all-night vigil for Shiva involving recitation, abhishekam, and fasting, and the stotra is one of the texts chanted through that night. Some reciters read it once daily as part of a regular Shiva practice; others take it up specifically on Mondays, traditionally associated with Shiva worship, or during the month of Shravan. Because of its demanding rhythm, it is also practised and performed as a spoken or sung recitation piece independent of ritual, including by classical musicians and dancers drawn to its structure. There is no single prescribed count attached to it the way there is with some mantras; practice generally follows personal or family custom, or the guidance of a priest, rather than a fixed rule. Many reciters pair it with an image or lingam of Shiva and simple offerings of water, bilva leaves, or incense, though the text does not itself specify ritual requirements beyond the act of recitation.
tradition: Within Shiva devotional tradition, the stotra's own closing verse states that one who recites, remembers, or speaks it attains ongoing purification and comes to firm devotion toward the guru, rather than following some other path, and that thinking of Shiva in this way removes confusion in embodied beings. A further verse attached to the text says that one who recites this hymn of Ravana's at the close of evening worship of Shiva is given a steady, generous fortune by Shiva, described through the traditional image of wealth accompanied by chariots, elephants, and horses. These are presented as statements made within the text itself about its own effect, attributed to the voice of the hymn and to the tradition that has carried it forward, rather than as claims made by any one teacher or commentator. The Shiv Tandav Stotram is held, in this way, to be both an act of praise and a declared means of approaching Shiva with devotion.

faq.q: Who wrote the Shiv Tandav Stotram?
faq.a: Tradition attributes it to Ravana, the king of Lanka from the Ramayana, composed as an offering of devotion to Shiva. No historical date or other biographical detail is recorded alongside this attribution; it is simply how the text has been transmitted and is named within its own closing line.

Most commonly in the evening, since the text's own closing verse ties it to evening worship of Shiva, and especially on Maha Shivaratri, when it is chanted through the night alongside other Shiva hymns. Many people also include it in Monday or Shravan month Shiva worship.

faq.q: Do I need a guru or initiation to recite it?
faq.a: No formal initiation is described in the text itself. It is widely recited by individuals as part of personal or family worship. Those wanting guidance on pronunciation or ritual accompaniment often turn to a local priest or an experienced reciter, simply for correctness rather than permission.

faq.q: Is the Shiv Tandav Stotram difficult to recite correctly?
faq.a: Its Sanskrit is dense and rhythmically demanding, with long compound words built to echo drumbeats, which is why many people first listen to a skilled reciter or recording before attempting it themselves, rather than reading it cold from a page.

faq.q: Is there a fixed number of times to recite the Shiv Tandav Stotram?
faq.a: No count is prescribed within the text itself. Practice varies - some recite it once daily, some only on Mondays or during Shivaratri - and this generally follows family custom or a priest's guidance rather than a rule stated in the stotra.
